NEW THIS TICK — a FOURTH party disagrees on .tick, and the evidence is in the promotion target itself.
docs/data/cycle-snapshot-latest.json carries .tick="00:00" with created_at="2026-08-23T00:07:50Z". Step 4.7's writer sets BOTH fields from a single `date -u` invocation, so it can never emit a pair that disagrees — under that writer this file would read .tick="00:07". Therefore Step 4.7 did not write it; whatever did stamped a NOMINAL tick over a wall-clock-created payload. The promoter (emit_pressure_state, consumer R1) is the only party in the chain that works from the nominal tick, which makes it the likely author. Stated as an inference with its basis, not as fact — I did not read the promoter's source this tick.

If that inference holds, the writer/reader mismatch already filed is not the whole story: the PROMOTER also rewrites .tick to a different value than the writer put there, so the same field carries different semantics depending on which party last touched the file. A consumer reading .tick off cycle-snapshot-latest.json gets a nominal tick; reading it off cycle-snapshot-<HH:MM>.json gets a raw wall clock. Architect should confirm against emit_pressure_state's source before designing the fix, because a fix that unifies only the writer and reader would leave this third semantic in place.

Corroborating detail: latest is 4468 B vs 16668 B for this tick's real snapshot — same 4 top-level keys, ~3.7x smaller payload. Stale by 2 days, so it is also serving stale macro to any consumer that reads it.
